paragraph_content.content: Availability constraints that are known in advance such as maintenance tasks should be considered in the scheduling. Aggoune (2004) first considered availability constraints for the job-shop scheduling problem but they did not study the flexible case. The FJSSP with non-fixed availability (FJSSP-nfa) was later introduced by Gao et al. (2006), where maintenance tasks have a deterministic duration and a time interval in which it must be scheduled. In the study, they solve the FJSSP-nfa with a hybrid genetic algorithm (Hybrid GA) on a small benchmark generated from classical FJSSP instances. Wang and Yu (2010) further explored the FJSSP-nfa and considered maintenance tasks with restricted maintenance resources and proposed a filtered beam search based heuristic algorithm. Rajkumar et al. (2011) solved the FJSSP-nfa with a greedy randomised adaptive search procedure algorithm and com pared their results to the literature.

Li and Pan (2012) and Li et al. (2014) presented a chemical-reaction optimization and a discrete artificial bee colony algorithm for the FJSSP-nfa. They considered potential multiple preventive maintenance tasks on machines while minimizing the makespan, the total work load and the maximum workload. They showed the efficiency of their approach by comparing their results to the literature on the same instances with diferent time windows. Ziaee (2014) designed an eficient heuristic algorithm based on a constructive procedure considering maintenance constraints that aims at producing reasonably good solutions very quickly that can be embedded in other solution approaches. El Khoukhi et al. (2017) considered unavailability periods on machines with fixed interval. They solved this problem with a dual-ants colony algorithm. Jing et al. (2017) studied probability basedpreventive maintenance. In this problem, they consider a probability of machine failure and process a preventive maintenance if the probability reaches a specific threshold. They solved this problem with a multi-objective GA. In a more recent study, Wang et al. (2021) considered both preventive maintenance and transportation process with energy consumption. They used a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm as a solution approach.

Besides the aforementioned works, the FJSSP-nfa has not seen much interest, which can partially be explained by the lack of benchmark instances. Indeed, all the works used a limited number of instances (less than 10) which does not allow a clear and fair comparison between approaches.

Most studies with maintenance constraints considered heuristic and meta-heuristic approaches. The eficiency of current days solvers (such as IBM CPLEX) and the lack of exact approaches led us to consider a MIP solution method to close the gap in the literature. Exact solution approaches can reach optimality on some instances which is valuable to evaluate the performance of non-exact methods such as meta-heuristics in later studies. To the best of our knowledge, no MIP model has been proposed in the literature for the FJSSP-nfa. Our first contribution is to propose a novel MIP formulation for the FJSSP-nfa. To evaluate the performance of our method we faced the lack of publicly available benchmarks for this problem with only a few instances from Gao et al. (2006) and Wang and Yu (2010). Our second contribution is to propose a large benchmark for the problem, generated from classical FJSSP benchmarks. The proposed benchmark is both di verse in terms of instance size and maintenance location on the horizon. A result comparison is performed to evaluate our approach and the impact of maintenance tasks in the scheduling process.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, the FJSSP-nfa is formally defined and a mixed integer formulation is proposed. Section 3 is devoted to describing the proposed benchmark and presenting the obtained results of the mixed integer formulation. The conclusion is to be found in Section 4.

To evaluate the performance of our proposed MIP, we carry out computational experiments on FJSSP-nfa instances. Previous works on this problem (Gao et al. (2006), Wang and Yu (2010)) used classical FJSSP instances with additional maintenance tasks as test instances, but very few instances are available for this problem in the literature. We first introduce a new benchmark for the FJSSP nfa using the well-known FJSSP instances. The instances are available on https://scheduling.cc.

The first parameter is the number of maintenance tasks to be scheduled on each machine. Each maintenance task is then defined with a processing time and a time window. The length of the time window must be greater than or equal to the processing time.

We select FJSSP instances from Brandimarte (1993), Kacem et al. (2002),Fattahi et al. (2007), Barnes and Chambers (1995), Dauz`ere-P´er`es and Paulli (1997), Behnke and Geiger (2012) and Hurink et al. (1994) as the basis instances. We solve each instance through a constraint pro gramming model to obtain a reasonably good makespan that is used to estimate the horizon for maintenance tasks. For each FJSSP instance, we generate 5 FJSSPnfa instances: 4 instances with only one maintenance task per machine whose time window is respectively within the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th quarter of the horizon, as well as a 5th instance with multiple maintenance tasks per machine. For the latter instances, the number of maintenance tasks on a machine is selected randomly with a uniform distribution between 1 and a quarter of the number of potential operations on that machine. In order to generate the time windows, the horizon is equally divided by the number of maintenance tasks. The start and end of each time window is then chosen randomly within each interval, such that the length of the time window is at least 1. Lastly, the duration of the maintenance tasks is generated randomly with a uniform distribution where the duration of the maintenance tasks is bounded by the length of the corresponding time window.

paragraph_content.content: We used multiple FJSSP benchmarks of 402 instances and generated 5 types of FJSSP-nfa instances (multiple maintenance tasks and one maintenance task with the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th quarter horizon) from each instance for a total of 2010 FJSSP-nfa instances. Table 3 gives a brief description of the FJSSP instances used. The reader is referred to Behnke and Geiger (2012) for more details. In the table, Nb. is the number of instances for this class, O the number of operations range, K the number of machines range. Flexibility describes the level of flexibility (number of machines available for an operation) of the instance: none if only one machine can process an operation, low if some operations can be processed on multiple machines, medium if most operations can be processed on multiple machines, high if most operations can be processed on most machines and total if any operation can be processed by any machine. Lastly MD describes whether the processing time of an operation is machine-dependant or not.

Once we have generated the benchmark, we solved each FJSSP-nfa instance using CPLEX on a Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 5120 CPU @ 2.20GHz CPU with a 3600-second timeout. Table 4 summarises the results obtained per class and type of instance. The classes of instances are the classical classes of FJSSP benchmarks and the type of instance is the maintenance task generation procedure (0 for instances with multiple maintenance tasks per machine, 1-4 for instances with only one maintenance task per machine and a reduced horizon). In each class, line “T” in column type combines types 0-4 for the corresponding class. For each type and class, Opt, Feas, NS are respectively the number of instances solved to optimality, the number of instances with a feasible solution and the number of instances with no solution found when the timeout was reached. CPU and Gap are respectively the average time spent solving and the average optimality gap obtained (in %) between the lower bound and the best solution obtained within the time limit.

The first observation is that the number of maintenance tasks and their position in the planing horizon does not have an important impact on the complexity as for each class of instance, results are very close over types 0-4 on average. Type 4 instances obtain the worst average optimality gap on 8 classes of instances. it can be concluded that having maintenance tasks in the last quarter of the planing horizon has negative efect on the MIP solving process. In the other hand, type 1 instances that has one maintenance task in the first quarter obtains the best average optimality gap on 5 classes of instance.

We can also observe that the flexibility can have an important impact on the complexity of an instance as class HurinkE has a total average optimality gap of 15.92% while HurinkR and HurinkV has respectively 30.07%

In Tables 5 and 6, we compare results between instances of diferent classes by grouping instances per number of operations and number of machines. Instances are grouped for better readability. Table 5 contains the results for instances having less than 100 operations. On the other hand, Table 6 contains the results for instances having more than 100 operations. O is the number of operations and K the number of machines. The size of the MIP (number of variables and constraints) depends on both O and K thus these groups tend to cluster instances per size. Of course, as we mentioned before, the complexity of an instance does not depend only on these two parameters.

Results show that our formulation solves instances with up to 36 operations and 6 machines to optimality in up to 90 seconds on average. Larger instances with up to 100 operations and 13 machines or 50 operations and 60 machines are solved with a reasonably good optimality gap within 3600 seconds for most instances. As shown in Table 5, all instances with less than 100 are solved and a feasible solution is obtained. Most larger instances with up to 225 operations and 16 machines are more tedious to solve even though some instances (150 operations with 11, 12 and 13 machines and 225 operations with 16, 17 and 18 machines) are much easier to solve due to the structure of the instance. The largest instances are too dificult to solve for the proposed formulation as we can only obtain solutions with a very high gap, or no solution at all within the time limit.

paragraph_content.content: In this study, we considered a flexible job shop scheduling problem under availability constraints. A MIP model has been proposed to solve the FJSSP-nfa. In order to test the proposed model, we introduced the first large bench mark for this problem and solved it. The experimental results shows the efectiveness of the model on small- and medium-sized instances.

As future research, we consider multiple perspectives. The solving process can be enhanced by designing good lower bounds or valid inequalities. Constraint programming is also a promising perspective with the recent works in this field.
